name: Napoleon III
role: President of the French Republic (1848-1852) and Emperor of the French (1852-1870)
summary: Napoleon III combined plebiscitary authoritarian rule, a strong executive and hereditary monarchy with state-led economic modernisation, free trade, public works and limited social reform. He presented himself as the heir of the Revolution and of Napoleon I, backed nationalities in Italy, protected the Pope's temporal power and expanded French influence overseas. In the 1860s he granted the legislature more powers and workers the right to strike.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: In his 1848 manifesto he warned against the state doing what private persons can do as well or better, and in 1860 argued that industry without competition stagnates and keeps prices high. His 1844 pamphlet, however, called industry a machine without a regulator, and he later directed railways, canals and credit through the state.

unions-good.rationale: His government drafted and carried the 1864 law on coalitions, which let workers and employers settle disputes between themselves, and he spoke of mutual-aid societies as reconciling classes. He never praised trade unions as such, and strikes stayed restricted when violent.

property-fundamental.rationale: His 1848 manifesto named religion, family and property 'the eternal bases of every social state' and called property's inviolability the foundation of civil liberty. In 1863 he guaranteed Arab landholders in Algeria their property.

regulate-corporations.rationale: In 1844 he described industry as running without rules and proposed that employers of more than ten workers be legally required to have an elected foreman; in the 1860s he instead sought freer commercial associations and fewer administrative controls.

cut-welfare.rationale: As president and emperor he promoted mutual-aid societies, subsidised relief, economy kitchens and aid for unemployment; in 1844 he proposed a state-funded colonies scheme for the poor. He never argued that relief breeds dependency.

worker-ownership.rationale: His 1844 plan made the poor members of an association farming wasteland collectively, aiming to make the working class 'proprietor'. Later he called schemes of this kind utopias and promoted mutual aid and private savings instead.

strong-leader.rationale: The 1852 constitution preamble deliberately gave the head of state an irresponsible-to-parliament executive, ministers who are only his auxiliaries, and removed legislative initiative and amendments because he judged parliamentary initiative and interpellations a source of abuse and sterile struggle.

state-harmful.rationale: In Napoleonic Ideas he wrote that a government is not 'a necessary ulcer' but 'the beneficent motive power of all social organization'.

empower-police-military.rationale: In 1867 he called for improving France's military institutions, with the argument that the stronger the country the more secure the peace, and proposed a mobile national guard.

decide-locally.rationale: His 1852 preamble defended administrative centralisation (prefects, a single central power) as the French tradition; in 1863 he announced a modest law to widen the powers of departmental and communal councils to correct 'excess of centralisation'.

traditional-family.rationale: His 1848 manifesto named religion, family and property as the eternal bases of every social state.

more-religion-public.rationale: At Bordeaux (1852) he promised to win the population 'to religion, morality and comfort'; he laid the first stone of Marseille cathedral and kept the Concordat. His school policy in the 1860s conflicted with the Church.

gradual-change.rationale: He wrote in 1867 that to govern is to use acquired experience and admit only progress compatible with national habits, and quoted Napoleon that a constitution is the work of time.

free-trade.rationale: He personally negotiated the 1860 Cobden-Chevalier treaty over industrialists' protests and in 1860 wrote that without competition industry stagnates. In 1867 he said free trade alone can secure supplies and level prices.

humanitarian-intervention.rationale: He told the legislature in 1861 that French troops went to Syria 'in the name of humanity' under a European convention to protect Christians.

revolution-justified.rationale: His 1852 preamble called revolutions a 'disastrous expedient', and in 1848 he said he would regard as enemies of the country those who sought to change by illegal means what France had established. He himself led armed coup attempts in 1836 and 1840 and seized power in 1851 (he said he left legality only to return to right), so the record is mixed.

experts-over-public.rationale: The 1852 constitution put law drafting in a Conseil d'Etat of 'practical men' and kept the elected body from amending bills, while he also kept universal suffrage and plebiscites as the final source of authority.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: His 1860 letter replaced the prohibitive system with moderate protective duties and free entry for raw materials, and the 1860 treaty cut duties on British goods despite industrial protest.

state-directs-investment.rationale: His January 1860 programme had the state lend capital to industry at moderate rates, fund drainage and land clearance, and build canals, roads and railways, and in 1852 he announced a Credit Foncier to ease borrowing on land.

widespread-small-property.rationale: In 1844 he called the extreme division of property ruinous to agriculture and wanted to recreate large-scale farming by association, yet also wanted to make the working class owners; in 1860 he planned to sell cleared communal land.

corporatist-bargaining.rationale: His 1844 pamphlet proposed legally recognised, worker-elected foremen (prud'hommes) and wages fixed by a balance between workers and employers under government direction; the 1864 coalitions law later left wages to free bargaining between them.

one-party-rule.rationale: On taking office in 1848 he asked to be 'men of the country, not of a party', and in 1852 said he was not 'of the family of ideologues'.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: In Napoleonic Ideas he saw in monarchy no divine right but valued the hereditary principle as a guarantee of a nation's integrity; he made the Empire hereditary in 1852 with his own plebiscite.

democracy-best.rationale: He wrote that no form of government is best a priori ('in politics the good is relative') and refused to rank monarchy against republic, yet he always grounded his power in universal suffrage and plebiscites.

direct-votes.rationale: He repeatedly appealed directly to the people by plebiscite (December 1851, 1852, 1870) on his regime and constitution, and wrote that nothing fundamental is done outside the people's will; ordinary laws stayed with the Corps legislatif.

natural-rulers.rationale: His 1852 preamble described the Senate as made up of the elements that create legitimate influence 'in every country': illustrious name, fortune, talent and service; Napoleonic Ideas presents great men as milestones of progress.

political-violence-never.rationale: He led armed coup attempts in 1836 and 1840, ordered the army to act in December 1851 and stated he would not recoil from any sacrifice to defeat 'factious' men; he also waged wars.

war-builds-character.rationale: In 1859 he said the war showed France had regained 'its ancient virtues'; but he repeatedly said war is made only by necessity and that 'the Empire is peace'.

separate-church-state.rationale: His 1852 preamble endorsed the Concordat as the settled regulation of relations between State and Church, and as president he approved the 1850-51 Falloux law that widened church influence in education.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: In his 1849 letter on restoring the Pope's temporal power he demanded a secularised administration, general amnesty, the Code Napoleon and liberal government.

military-superiority.rationale: In 1867 he argued that France must perfect its military organisation, arms and navy because 'the stronger we are, the more secure the peace'.

class-struggle-history.rationale: He told industrialists in 1849 to teach workers that the rich man's interest is not opposed to the poor man's, and called mutual aid societies a means to reconcile classes. He presented progress as driven by providence and great leaders.

equal-outcomes.rationale: His 1848 manifesto wanted industrial reforms that aim 'not to ruin the rich for the benefit of the poor but to found each one's well-being on the prosperity of all'.

industrial-civilization-disaster.rationale: In 1844 he said industry devours its children but asked whether to kill it 'because it kills' and answered that its benefits are immense and only its victims should be cared for; later he promoted industry, railways and expositions.

restore-past-order.rationale: He wrote that restoring the ancien regime would have been folly and that progress 'never retreats'; his 1852 preamble said nothing of the old order remained but great memories.

results-over-ideology.rationale: In 1852 he said France supported him because he was not of the 'family of ideologues' and that it needs confidence and security rather than new systems; Napoleonic Ideas praises adapting a system to events.

direct-action.rationale: In June 1849 he called the insurgents against a government 'legitimate because produced by universal suffrage' factious; he favoured appeals to the ballot and plebiscite.

profit-exploitation.rationale: In 1844 he described the working class as helots among Sybarites and the employer as the oppressor, but in 1849 he told employers to make a just share for labour and said the rich man's interest is not opposed to the poor's.

collective-farming.rationale: His 1844 pamphlet proposed state-financed agricultural colonies on 6 million hectares of wasteland, worked by workers' associations rather than individual farmers; he did not later pursue the scheme.

taxation-theft.rationale: In 1844 he approved the saying that tax properly spent is the best of investments; as ruler he levied taxes and budgeted, promising in 1861 to avoid new taxes.

conscription.rationale: In 1848 he promised to maintain the fundamental laws of French military organisation while easing conscription; in 1867 he proposed only modifications to the 1832 law and a mobile guard.

total-state.rationale: His 1848 manifesto warned against the tendency of the State to do what individuals can do as well or better, and in 1865 he said he worked to reduce obstacles to individual initiative.

territorial-expansion.rationale: In 1859 he said one is greater today by moral influence than by sterile conquests, but he annexed Savoy and Nice in 1860, took Cochinchina and defended his Mexican and Asian expeditions in 1863 as needed to keep French influence.

avoid-deficit-stimulus.rationale: In 1859 and 1861 he proudly reported balanced budgets without new loans, but his large public works ran deficits.

national-self-determination.rationale: In 1859 he told Italians he would not impose his will and that his army would not obstruct 'the free expression of your legitimate wishes'; in 1864 France argued for the nationality principle and the right of populations to be consulted. His Mexican and Algerian policies cut against this.

reason-over-faith.rationale: He credited 'Providence' and religion for order, and in 1844 called the right appeal one 'to reason and heart'.

class-collaboration.rationale: In 1850 he said mutual aid societies reconcile classes and bring rich and worker together; in 1849 he told industrialists to show workers that the interest of the rich is not opposed to the poor's.

state-class-instrument.rationale: He said a government resting on the will of the masses is slave to no party, and in Napoleonic Ideas called government a beneficent social motive power.

night-watchman-state.rationale: As president and emperor he ran state railways and public-works programmes, a state credit system, relief schemes and public education, and in 1844 proposed a state-funded colonisation to end poverty.

discourage-race-mixing.rationale: In 1865 he hoped the Arab race 'regenerated and merged with the French race' might regain individuality, as the Gauls merged with Romans.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: In 1851 he said his system rebuilds authority 'without hurting equality'; Napoleonic Ideas praises equality of rights before the law. In Algeria he claimed the right to be masters because more civilised.

uniform-civil-code.rationale: His 1852 preamble praised the Code Napoleon regulating all citizens' interests and the end of separate religious jurisdictions; he urged it for the Papal States in 1849. In Algeria he respected Muslim religion and property.

no-religion-state-schools.rationale: In 1848 he promised freedom of teaching alongside protecting religion, and approved the 1850-51 Falloux law; later his minister Duruy clashed with the Church.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Wrote that the people are masters of their destiny and used plebiscites, but took power in a coup and ratified it by plebiscite under repression; mixed.

trade-surplus.rationale: His 1844 pamphlet argued that the home market matters more than exports, and later he lowered tariffs and welcomed imports.

ban-extremist-parties.rationale: He called those who sought to change by illegal means enemies of the country in 1848, and after 1851 repressed republican opposition, arresting about 26,000.

separated-powers.rationale: His 1852 constitution created a Conseil d'Etat, Corps legislatif and Senate, with the Senate able to annul arbitrary acts; but he concentrated responsibility and executive control in the head of state and rejected parliamentary checks on ministers.

priority-to-poor.rationale: In 1844 he wrote that naturally in misfortune one thinks of those who suffer and proposed a plan for the poorest class; in 1867 he called for measures to make the lot of the greatest number prosperous.

restrict-strikes-picketing.rationale: His government introduced the 1864 law on coalitions, repealing the ban on strikes, and in 1865 he said workers and employers had learned to settle their disputes between themselves.

population-causes-poverty.rationale: In 1844 he blamed poverty on 'organic' vices in agriculture, industry, commerce and taxation and said it could be cured by reorganisation of work and land.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: He said in December 1851 that he had left legality only to return to right, after dissolving the Assembly; about 26,000 were arrested, and the 1852 constitution kept the army's passive obedience.

price-controls-essentials.rationale: In 1867, after a poor harvest, he said 'free trade alone can ensure supplies and level prices', and he decreed freedom of the bakery trade.

party-controls-media.rationale: His 1852 decree required government authorisation for political papers and allowed suspensions; in 1867 he announced a law to give press offences to the courts and end the government's discretionary power.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: Napoleonic Ideas, in his own voice, presents a European association with a common code and court of cassation as the aim of Napoleon; as ruler he proposed only a congress of sovereigns (1863).

common-currency.rationale: Napoleonic Ideas praises a uniform European coinage and weights, and his 1860 letter to Victor Emmanuel proposed an Italian confederation with one flag, customs system and currency.

head-commands-forces.rationale: In 1850 he said he alone disposes of the army under the constitution, and the 1852 constitution made ministers dependent only on the head of state.

clerical-rule.rationale: In 1849 he told Pope Pius IX's restored government to secularise the administration and adopt liberal institutions, and his 1852 preamble kept the clergy in the Concordat framework.

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: He allied with Britain in the Crimean War, with Piedmont in 1859, and kept a French garrison in Rome from 1849 to 1870.

rural-life-healthier.rationale: In 1844 he wrote that industry drains men into the cities and enervates them and that those in excess in towns should be recalled to the countryside to 'retemper' mind and body in the open air.

reunify-divided-nation.rationale: In 1859 he fought to free northern Italy from Austria and in 1866 he said he detested the 1815 treaties on which others wanted to base policy.

cultures-equal-different.rationale: In 1865 he proclaimed that in Algeria 'we must be masters because we are the most civilised'.

constituent-assembly.rationale: The 1852 constitution was drafted by a commission he chose and ratified by plebiscite, after he dissolved the elected Assembly.

restrict-freedoms-for-growth.rationale: In December 1851 he said a system that rebuilds authority is the only edifice able later to bear wise liberty, and in 1852 he promised conquests of waste land, roads, ports and railways, while censoring the press from February 1852.

direct-election-head-of-state.rationale: He was elected president by direct universal suffrage in 1848 and later wrote that the chief elected by the people is responsible to them; he then made the title hereditary.

property-serves-common-good.rationale: He called property's inviolability a basis of civil liberty and said the State must protect it, not condition it.

collective-defense.rationale: In 1859 he said that when Austria attacked Piedmont, 'the honour and interests of France made it a duty' to support his ally, and sent troops.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: Napoleonic Ideas praises Napoleon for re-establishing the clergy 'without making them a means of government', and he kept the Concordat; yet he also favoured the Church in education.

nonpartisan-head-of-state.rationale: In 1848 he asked to be a man of the country, not of a party; in 1867 he spoke of keeping fundamental laws above controversy and hostile passions. He remained an executive ruler.

sacred-ruler.rationale: In Napoleonic Ideas he saw in monarchy 'neither the principle of divine right' nor its alleged defects.

character-from-environment.rationale: In Napoleonic Ideas he wrote that man obeys all his life the impressions and trials of his early years, and in 1844 that a man is what his function obliges him to be.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: He said he was responsible to the people and would respect their verdict, yet in December 1851 he acted outside the constitution.

mixed-constitution.rationale: Napoleonic Ideas argued that a great state needs both a hereditary family or aristocracy for permanent interests and representatives of the people for transient ones; his Empire joined a hereditary emperor, Senate and elected Corps legislatif.

leader-cult.rationale: He promoted Napoleon I's memory in public life and accepted public acclamations, presenting him in 1839 as the 'Messiah of new ideas'.

economic-self-sufficiency.rationale: His 1860 policy opened France to imports and he repeatedly championed free trade.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: He praised the end of privileged classes in 1852 but made his own title hereditary and praised Napoleon for restoring titles without privilege.

civilizing-tutelage.rationale: In 1865 he told Algeria's settlers that 'we must be masters because we are the most civilised', and told Arabs he would make them share 'the benefits of civilisation'.

armed-group-creates-revolution.rationale: He led armed attempts at Strasbourg (1836) and Boulogne (1840) with a small group, hoping troops would rally to him; both failed.

national-mission.rationale: In Napoleonic Ideas he wrote that France is 'the fountain of progress for Western Europe' with a mission, and in 1849 that French armies had left abolition of feudal abuses and germs of liberty wherever they went.
